text: I’ll model the fluid directly in metres as a 60 mm extrusion. Its cross-section is the 0.05 mm radial annulus plus a centered 12 mm-wide keyway reaching 5 mm radially into the 40 mm shaft. The shaft steps define the two axial openings but lie outside this sealed fluid domain, so the high- and low-pressure patches are the two end cross-sections. For this very thin clearance, I’ll use a swept mesh rather than isotropic tetrahedra. First I’m constructing and measuring a coarse CAD model.

The first volume check exposed a construction issue: `Box` was centered by default, so its nominal placement did not put the keyway floor at the requested 5 mm depth. I’ll correct the cutter using explicit alignments, then identify the eight resulting faces by their intrinsic geometry and render the fluid before exporting anything.

The corrected preview shows the intended connected leakage path: a thin annulus surrounding the shaft and the much deeper longitudinal keyway at the top. The CAD volume is one solid with exactly seven faces: outer bore cylinder, inner shaft cylinder, two end faces, keyway floor, and two keyway flanks. I’ll now bind those design-created faces to the five requested patch names and export them together so their STL seams share identical vertices. I assign +Z to the stated 50 mm/high-pressure end and −Z to the 30 mm/low-pressure end.

For the production mesh I’ll generate the cross-section directly in Gmsh from the same dimensions, refine the 0.05 mm annulus to approximately one element through the clearance and about 0.05–0.1 mm tangentially, then sweep it through 60 mm with 30 axial layers. This avoids the enormous cell count and unreliable gap capture of an isotropic 3-D mesher while retaining the keyway as part of the same connected fluid region.

Gmsh represents the swept curved walls as generic “Surface of Extrusion” entities rather than as OCC cylinders, so the intended analytic-type classifier was too strict; no mesh was written. I’ll rebuild the Gmsh model and inspect the sweep’s returned surface order, areas, and centers before assigning physical groups.

The inspection shows the outer bore is one swept curved face, while the notched shaft’s remaining circular boundary is split into two swept curved faces by the keyway opening; together their areas exactly reproduce the CAD shaft area. The three planar swept faces are the floor and flanks. I’ll use those topology facts, build the volume mesh, and write it in Gmsh 2.2 format for OpenFOAM conversion.

The swept mesh contains 23,220 prism cells (30 axial layers) and matches the CAD patch areas. I’ll convert it to OpenFOAM, inspect the imported boundary names and cell statistics, then render a cutaway to verify that both annulus and keyway are populated.

Conversion requires a minimal OpenFOAM `system/controlDict`; the Gmsh mesh itself is complete and unchanged. I’ll add only that required case metadata (no solver or boundary-condition files), then repeat conversion and the binding `checkMesh`.

The conversion succeeded and all five patch names and 23,220 prism cells are present. `checkMesh` stopped before inspecting geometry because this OpenFOAM build also expects empty `fvSchemes`/`fvSolution` dictionaries even for mesh checking. I’ll add only those required dictionaries, repeat conversion so the build script is self-contained, and rerun the check.

The binding check passes: one connected region, 23,220 prisms, all five requested patches, positive volumes, acceptable skewness, and `Mesh OK`. The total meshed volume is 3.75726×10⁻⁶ m³ versus 3.75845×10⁻⁶ m³ CAD (0.032% low from circular discretization). I’ll now make a cutaway mesh image and inspect the end cross-section to confirm the thin annulus remains connected to the deeper keyway.

The final visual inspection confirms the intended topology: the 0.05 mm annulus is present around the full circumference (one prism through its thickness), and it opens continuously into the resolved 12 mm × 5 mm keyway. The keyway has multiple cells through both width and depth, while 30 swept layers resolve the 60 mm leakage direction.

The `location_in_mesh` advisory is inapplicable here: this is a direct Gmsh volume mesh of the exact fluid cross-section, not a snappyHexMesh inside/outside selection. I’ll waive that advisory for this reason and finalize.
